content: 1. Irlam J, Visser MM, Rollins NN, and Siegfried N conducted a systematic review on micronutrient supplementation in children and adults living with HIV infection. This review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2010 (Issue 12, CD003650). 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) released guidelines in 2011 for intensified tuberculosis case-finding and isoniazid preventive therapy for individuals living with HIV in resource-limited settings. 3. Kerac M and colleagues analyzed the prevalence of wasting among infants under six months of age in developing countries. They also examined the implications of new case definitions based on WHO growth standards. This secondary data analysis was published in the Archives of Disease in Childhood in 2011 (Volume 96, Pages 1008–1013). 4. Kerac M and colleagues provided a background review on admission and discharge criteria for managing severe acute malnutrition in infants under six months of age. This document is available as a PDF. 5. Kerac M and colleagues also reviewed inpatient treatment protocols for severe acute malnutrition in infants under six months of age. This document is also available as a PDF. 6. Nyeko R, Kalyesubula I, Mworozzi E, and Bachou H investigated lactose intolerance in severely malnourished children with diarrhea admitted to the nutrition unit at Mulago Hospital in Uganda. Their findings were published in BMC Pediatrics in 2010 (Volume 10, Article 31). 7. Kukuruzovic R and Brewster D conducted a randomized trial comparing milk formulas in the treatment of acute gastroenteritis and malnutrition. Their study was published in the Journal of Child Health in 2002 (Volume 38, Pages 571–577). 8. Vasquez-Garibay E, Méndez-Estrada C, Romero-Velarde E, García-Iglesias MT, and Campollo-Rivas O demonstrated that nutritional support with nucleotide addition enhances immune response in severely malnourished infants. This research was published in Archives of Medical Research in 2004 (Volume 35, Pages 284–288). 9. Hossain M, Hassan MQ, Rahman MH, Kabir AR, Hannan AH, and Rahman AK compared hospital management of severely malnourished children using a locally adapted protocol versus the WHO protocol. Their findings were published in Indian Pediatrics in 2009 (Volume 46, Pages 213–217). 10. Wilkinson C and Isanaka S compared diluted F100 formula with infant formula in the treatment of severely malnourished infants under six months of age. This study was accessed on August 16, 2013. 11. The WHO published guiding principles in 2005 for feeding non-breastfed children aged 6–24 months. 12. The WHO also developed an integrated course on infant and young child feeding counseling in 2006. 13. A WHO consultation in 2004 reviewed the current literature on severe malnutrition. The report was published in 2005. 14. The WHO's 47th edition of basic documents was accessed on November 7, 2013. 15. The WHO issued guidelines in 2010 for the declaration of interests by experts. 16. A double-blind study conducted in a high HIV prevalence setting, where most children had kwashiorkor, evaluated the use of antibiotics (amoxicillin/cefdinir) in children with uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition. The response to antibiotics may have been influenced by the high prevalence of HIV and kwashiorkor. 17. A question was raised regarding the use of high-dose versus low-dose vitamin A supplementation in children with severe acute malnutrition. Randomized trials showed varying results due to differences in malnutrition criteria, supplementation duration, and classifications of diarrhea types. 18. The use of low-osmolarity oral rehydration solution (ORS) versus standard-osmolarity ORS in children with severe acute malnutrition and dehydration was evaluated. Studies showed consistent results despite moderate to high statistical heterogeneity. 19. The use of half-strength Darrow’s solution with 5% dextrose versus Ringer’s lactate in children with severe acute malnutrition and shock was assessed. Limitations included small sample sizes, non-blinded studies, and restricted follow-up to the hospitalization period. 20. The WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guidelines Development includes experts in maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health, chronic diseases, food safety, and global health programs. 21. The Nutrition Guidance Advisory Group Subgroup on Nutrition in the Life Course and Undernutrition (2010–2012) included experts in severe malnutrition, pediatric care, and program management from various international institutions. 22. External experts and stakeholders contributed to the WHO guidelines, including professionals from academic institutions, humanitarian organizations, and public health agencies. 23. The WHO summarized considerations for determining the strength of recommendations for managing severe acute malnutrition in children aged 6–59 months. These included benefits such as reduced mortality, improved outcomes, and cost considerations, as well as potential risks like overdiagnosis and antibiotic resistance.
